title: "How to get fit over 40, one habit at a time."
slug: "how-to-get-fit-over-40"
excerpt: "To get fit over 40, begin with activity you can repeat, build up gradually and choose something you enjoy. You do not need to recreate the training you did at 20. Start with your current week, your recent activity and a reason to keep going."
author: "Attic Jiu Jitsu"
categories: ["Fitness"]
seo_title: "How to Get Fit Over 40: A Beginner’s Guide | Attic"
description: "Getting fit after 40 starts with a routine you can repeat. Compare walking, strength work and classes, with practical next steps for beginners in Carlow."
noindex: false
source_id: "attic-seo-guides-v1/how-to-get-fit-over-40"
source_commit: "0527a72acbb7817ea2c5fa5ea52aa68b28b88471"

## Start with the week you actually have.

Write down when you could realistically be active around work, family and travel. A short walk on a lunch break, a class on an evening you are usually free or a regular weekend activity gives you something concrete to arrange.

Then identify the obstacle that has stopped previous attempts. Was it boredom, inconvenient times, cost, uncertainty about exercises or doing too much at once? Choose a solution to that obstacle before buying equipment or a long membership.

## Include activity for stamina and strength.

Ireland’s Every Move Counts guidelines advise adults aged 18–64 to work towards 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity, per week, alongside muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days. These are goals to build towards, not a first-week challenge.

Walking, swimming, cycling, gym sessions and coached sports offer different ways to be active. Choose a combination that fits your preferences. A sport session includes explanations and breaks, so its entire duration should not automatically be counted as vigorous exercise.

## Pick an activity you want to return to.

If machines and solo workouts do not appeal, try an activity with a skill to learn. Dance, a running group or a beginner martial arts class can give you an appointment and people to see. If close physical contact is unappealing, choose an option that avoids it.

At Attic in Carlow, the activity is Brazilian jiu-jitsu. You practise movement and positions with a partner under a coach’s instruction. It is one possible route into regular activity, rather than a complete fitness prescription for everyone.

[Getting fit with jiu-jitsu in Carlow](/fitness-classes-carlow)

[Explore alternatives to a gym routine](/blog/get-fit-without-a-gym)

## Men and women can need different starting conversations.

A man returning after years of desk work may need to set aside his old sporting pace. A woman returning to exercise may want clarity about class culture, symptoms affecting activity or whether she prefers mixed or women-only sessions. Neither group has one universal fitness level.

Use your circumstances to choose your first step. If an injury, medical condition or symptoms make you uncertain about exercise, ask your GP or physiotherapist for individual advice before contact training.

[Getting fit over 40 for men](/blog/fitness-for-men-over-40)

[Getting fit over 40 for women](/blog/fitness-for-women-over-40)

## Measure consistency before performance.

After a few weeks, review whether you are attending, whether the activity interests you and whether the routine works with the rest of life. Those answers tell you more about its sustainability than one exhausting session.

If you want to explore jiu-jitsu, check the beginner timetable and ask the academy how the first session works. Explain your current level and your goal of becoming more active. You can learn about a class before deciding to join.

[Beginner jiu-jitsu in Carlow](/beginners-bjj-carlow)

slug: "fitness-for-men-over-40"
excerpt: "For men getting fit over 40, a useful first move is to stop treating your old fitness level as today’s starting point. Pick an activity that fits your present life and decide when you will actually do it. Build from there."

## Separate past experience from current capacity.

Having played football, lifted weights or trained hard in your twenties can make it tempting to resume where you stopped. Your recent activity is a more useful starting point than an old personal best.

Tell a coach what you have been doing lately, rather than only what you used to do. If you have been largely inactive or have a condition that affects exercise, discuss a suitable starting point with your GP or physiotherapist. An introductory class is not a medical assessment.

## Solve the diary problem first.

Look at a normal work week. If you regularly miss evening plans because of commuting or family commitments, an ambitious evening programme may be a poor fit. Start by identifying a reliable gap, then choose an activity that fits it.

The HSE encourages fitting movement into everyday life and beginning with small amounts. A walk during a break, an active journey or a planned class can each have a place. Avoid building a routine that only works in an unusually quiet week.

## Consider a group if training alone does not stick.

For some people, deciding what to do in the gym is another task after a long working day. A coached class provides a lesson and a starting time. Partner practice can also make a sport feel different from another solo workout.

Jiu-jitsu is one option to explore. You work through positions and movements with another person, and the technical problem gives the session its focus. It involves close contact, which is an important part of deciding whether it is for you.

[Getting fit with jiu-jitsu in Carlow](/fitness-classes-carlow)

[Other ways to get active without a gym routine](/blog/get-fit-without-a-gym)

## Replace proving yourself with learning.

If you try a new sport, being a beginner is part of the activity. You do not need to win a practice round or keep up with someone who has trained for years. Ask questions about pace, partner work and anything you do not understand.

At Attic, tell the coach if fitness and recreation are your priorities. Competition is a separate decision. The first useful outcome is understanding the class and deciding whether you want to come back, not measuring yourself against the room.

[Questions to ask before starting BJJ over 40](/blog/starting-bjj-over-40)

## Make one clear next step in Carlow.

Compare the timetable with your diary, look at the current beginner programme and contact the academy with your experience and availability. Ask what a first session requires before buying gear.

If the schedule does not fit, choose another workable activity rather than abandoning the aim of getting active. Your plan should serve your week, not depend on changing every part of it at once.

excerpt: "Getting fit over 40 as a woman starts with choosing activity that suits your life, preferences and current health. You might be trying exercise for the first time, returning after a break or looking for a sport you enjoy more than the gym."

## Choose a goal beyond how you look.

Ask what you want your week to feel like: time away from work, an active hobby, something social or a skill that takes your full attention. A specific reason helps you judge whether an activity is worth returning to.

Compare practical details too. Can you attend at the advertised time? Do you prefer being outdoors, exercising privately or joining a group? Would partner contact make a session interesting or uncomfortable? These preferences are useful information, not obstacles to push aside.

## If perimenopause or menopause affects your plans.

The HSE recommends regular exercise, including weight-bearing and resistance activities, as part of looking after health during menopause. If symptoms worry you or affect what feels manageable, speak with your GP rather than trying to solve everything through a class.

A sports coach can explain their programme and discuss how a lesson works. That does not make a martial arts class specialist menopause care. Ask an appropriately qualified health professional about pregnancy, recovery after childbirth or other conditions that affect exercise choices.

## Find out whether the environment feels right.

Before joining any group, ask how beginners are introduced, who teaches, what a lesson involves and whether a visit is possible. For a contact sport, ask how training partners and personal boundaries are handled.

If a women-only group matters to you, check it explicitly. Attic’s published catalogue has adult beginner and mixed-level classes; our women’s introduction page does not promise a separate women-only programme. You should know the format before choosing it.

[Jiu-jitsu for women in Carlow](/womens-bjj-carlow)

## Where jiu-jitsu could fit.

Brazilian jiu-jitsu gives exercise a technical focus: learning a position, practising a movement and working with a partner. At Attic in Carlow, there are beginner gi and no-gi options to ask about.

That may appeal if you want to learn a sport and meet people. If you want non-contact exercise, consider walking, swimming, dance or an appropriate strength class instead. Choose an activity you want to repeat rather than one you feel you ought to enjoy.

[Getting fit with jiu-jitsu in Carlow](/fitness-classes-carlow)

[Compare activities beyond the gym](/blog/get-fit-without-a-gym)

## Build a routine around what is realistic.

Start with a workable commitment and review how it feels alongside the rest of your week. Make space to rest and change your plan if work, symptoms or family responsibilities shift.

For jiu-jitsu, contact the academy with your recent activity and the class times that might suit you. Ask about equipment, the beginner programme and the first visit. There is no need to decide on a long-term sporting goal before learning what the class is like.

slug: "get-fit-without-a-gym"

## Work out what you dislike about the gym.

Boredom, uncertainty and feeling uncomfortable are different problems. If you dislike repeating movements alone, a social activity may help. If you are unsure what to do, a coached session gives you structure. If you dislike indoor settings, start outdoors.

Be specific so your next choice changes the part that was not working. Replacing one inconvenient membership with another is unlikely to solve a diary or travel problem.

## Compare a few different ways to be active.

Think about what you want from the activity before deciding how demanding it should be. Consider the cost, travel, equipment and whether you prefer a fixed appointment or the flexibility to start whenever you are free.

- Walking or cycling: useful to explore if you prefer flexible activity or being outdoors.
- Swimming: an option if you enjoy being in the water and can attend pool sessions.
- Dance or a group exercise class: an option if music and a shared routine interest you.
- Strength training with instruction: an option if your main interest is learning resistance exercises.
- A coached sport: an option if learning a skill and practising with others helps you stay interested.

## Why some people prefer learning a sport.

A sport gives you a question to work on during the session. In jiu-jitsu, that might be where to move from a position or how to practise the technique just demonstrated. The exercise happens through the activity rather than being the only thing you focus on.

There is also a scheduled lesson and a group of people practising alongside you. If that appeals, ask a club about a beginner session. If you prefer solo activity, there is no reason to force a group sport into your plan.

[Getting fit with jiu-jitsu in Carlow](/fitness-classes-carlow)

## Check what a martial arts class actually involves.

Jiu-jitsu uses close partner contact and grappling. It is a different experience from a non-contact fitness class or an individual weights session. Ask what you will practise, how beginners are introduced and what clothing you need.

It is reasonable to decide it does not suit you. A fitness choice should fit your needs, and other activities may offer a better starting point if you need low-contact or individually prescribed exercise.

[Beginner jiu-jitsu in Carlow](/beginners-bjj-carlow)

## Try a manageable next step in Carlow.

Choose one option and find out the arrangements for a first visit. The HSE’s Get Active programme is another starting resource: it provides a gradual walking and muscle-strengthening plan for people building activity levels.

For Attic, check the timetable and send an enquiry about a suitable beginner session. The team can confirm availability and introductory arrangements. Look for an activity you want to repeat, rather than judging success by how exhausted the first session makes you.

[Check Attic’s current timetable](/classes#live-schedule)

slug: "starting-bjj-over-40"
excerpt: "You can enquire about starting BJJ over 40 without already knowing the techniques or wanting to compete. The important conversation is whether contact training suits your current health, how the academy introduces beginners and what routine you can sustain."

## Your recent activity matters more than an age label.

Two people in their forties can have very different starting points. One may already play sport several times a week; another may be trying exercise after years away. Explain your situation rather than expecting an age alone to tell the coach what you need.

If you have a health condition, persistent pain or an injury that could be affected by grappling, ask your GP or physiotherapist about suitability first. A coach can explain a class, but cannot replace individual medical advice.

## Understand partner practice before joining in.

Brazilian jiu-jitsu is a contact sport. You learn positions and techniques with a partner, and live practice can involve changing pressure and resistance. Ask how a beginner is introduced to each part of the lesson.

Learn the academy’s stopping signals and tapping etiquette before practising submissions. Ask the coach when you are uncertain, communicate with your partner and stop an exercise if something feels wrong. No sport can promise injury-free training.

## Choose learning over keeping up.

Your first challenge may be remembering unfamiliar positions, not producing more effort. Try to understand the demonstration and the purpose of the practice before worrying about speed or how experienced students perform.

Discuss pace and breaks with the coach. You do not need to prove that an old sporting background makes you an advanced grappler. Being comfortable asking a basic question is useful when learning anything new.

## Plan around recovery and ordinary life.

Compare the beginner timetable with work, family responsibilities and other activity. Leave enough space to see how the new sport feels rather than immediately filling every available evening.

Regular attendance is useful only if the schedule remains workable. Ask about the current beginner programme and what happens after it, including ongoing membership and whether you want to continue gi, no-gi or both.

[How to get fit over 40](/blog/how-to-get-fit-over-40)

[Compare beginner and ongoing plans](/memberships)

## Questions to ask before your first class.

A clear first conversation helps you decide whether the class is right for you. At Attic, explain that you are a complete beginner and tell the team which session times might work.

- Which class should I start with, and how is partner work introduced?
- What should I wear and bring?
- How do I stop an exercise or ask to sit out?
- What equipment does the current beginner programme include?
- How are my first session and start date confirmed?

## Gi and no-gi use different clothing.

A gi is the training jacket and trousers used in traditional Brazilian jiu-jitsu classes, worn with a belt. No-gi classes train without that jacket and trousers, using appropriate sportswear instead. The academy can explain what your selected session requires.

For an introductory visit, ask whether there are clothing or equipment arrangements for first-timers. Do not assume loan gear is available or that ordinary clothes are suitable for every session.

## A useful first-visit checklist.

Prepare for close partner practice as well as exercise. Confirm any specific academy rules with the team; the list below is a starting point for that conversation.

- Bring water and suitable clean training clothing, as confirmed by the coach.
- Trim nails and remove jewellery before partner practice.
- Ask whether clothing with pockets, zips or hard fasteners is unsuitable.
- Bring footwear for use away from the training mats and follow the academy’s mat rules.
- Tell the coach that you are new and ask before joining an exercise you do not understand.

## Confirm the session and allow time for questions.

Check the current timetable, then contact the academy about your first class. A website enquiry starts that conversation; it does not reserve a place or confirm introductory pricing.

Attic is at 4 Charlotte Street, Graigue, Carlow, R93 D431. Use that full address when planning your journey and ask when the team would like you to arrive. If you are bringing a child, confirm the age group and parent or guardian arrangements too.

[Check class times](/classes#live-schedule)

[Kids martial arts in Carlow](/kids-martial-arts-carlow)

## What about the beginner pack?

The published adult beginner programme includes training and a kimono, white belt and bag. A separate kids beginner pack is also listed. Check the current plan details and how equipment is arranged before purchasing.

Ask about sizing, availability and whether any additional clothing is needed. A programme that includes a gi does not automatically answer what to wear under it or what to wear for no-gi training.

[Beginner jiu-jitsu in Carlow](/beginners-bjj-carlow)

[Current programme details and prices](/memberships)

## You can arrive without knowing the terminology.

A beginner lesson introduces unfamiliar positions and movements. Listen to the demonstration and ask the coach to explain anything unclear, especially how to stop practice or communicate with a partner.

Treat the visit as an introduction to the activity. Afterwards, consider whether the lesson, environment and journey work for you. That is more useful than expecting to feel accomplished after one class.

## What children do in a jiu-jitsu class.

Brazilian jiu-jitsu is a grappling art. Students practise positions and movement with a partner, rather than learning striking combinations. A youth programme should use coaching and activities appropriate to the children in the group.

At Attic, the published kids class is for ages 6–11 and the teen class is for ages 12–15. Ask about the appropriate group if your child is near an age boundary or has specific needs.

[Kids martial arts in Carlow](/kids-martial-arts-carlow)

[Teen classes for ages 12–15](/teens-jiu-jitsu-carlow)

## Think in terms of practice, rather than promises.

A class gives children opportunities to listen, take turns, try a movement again and work with a partner. Those experiences can be worthwhile, but no academy can guarantee confidence, concentration or a particular personality change on a timetable.

Your child’s response matters. Ask what they enjoyed, what felt difficult and whether they would like another visit. A nervous first session is not a complete verdict, but persistent discomfort deserves attention.

## Questions to ask the academy.

Speak with the team before enrolling and ask about the current arrangements rather than assuming that every club runs the same way.

- Who teaches this age group, and how are new children introduced?
- What partner contact and techniques are included?
- What are the safeguarding, vetting and supervision arrangements?
- Can a parent observe, and what are the collection arrangements?
- How do you respond if a child wants to stop or is uncomfortable?
- What equipment is needed, and what does the current membership cover?

## If bullying is the reason you are looking.

Tell the coach about your concern, but do not place responsibility for solving bullying on your child’s sporting performance. Work with the school and appropriate support services, and encourage your child to seek help from a trusted adult.

A supervised grappling class is different from an unsafe confrontation. Martial arts should not be presented as a guarantee that a child can handle bullying alone.

## Check the practical fit for your family.

Look at the current timetable, travel and school commitments together. Compare beginner equipment packs with ongoing kids memberships, and ask about family coverage if siblings or a parent are interested too.

At Attic, adult and youth sessions follow their appropriate groups. A family plan does not mean everyone shares a lesson or that childcare is provided while a parent trains. Clarifying those details helps you choose an activity that works beyond the first visit.

## Compare like with like.

A monthly membership, a fixed beginner programme and occasional training access are different products. Before comparing the headline number, check how long access lasts, how many classes it covers and who is eligible.

Also check whether a plan is for kids, teens, students or adults. A lower price may reflect different access or eligibility rather than the same training being available more cheaply.

## Include equipment in the starting cost.

Gi training needs a suitable jacket, trousers and belt. No-gi uses different sportswear, so ask what is required for the class you intend to attend. Avoid buying equipment until the academy has explained its requirements.

Attic’s published adult beginner programme includes a kimono, white belt and bag alongside the introductory training. The separate kids beginner pack also lists equipment. Check current details, sizing and arrangements directly before choosing a pack.

Check the ongoing option as well as the beginner offer. Ask what happens at the end of an introductory programme and confirm how membership, payments and your start date are arranged.

[Student training in Carlow](/students)

## Family coverage needs a direct check.

An adult-and-child or sibling option may make sense for some households, while another family may need different coverage. Tell the team who wants to train and their ages so they can explain the relevant plan.

Then check the timetable. A shared membership is useful only if the appropriate sessions work for the people covered. Do not assume that children and adults can train together or that their classes run at the same time.

[Family memberships and training](/family-martial-arts-carlow)

## Budget for the routine, not just the first payment.

Add the journey and the time needed to attend. If you are coming from Athy or Kilkenny, repeated travel can be a meaningful part of the commitment even when the membership itself fits your budget.

Before joining, ask about class availability, equipment, eligibility, payment terms and any introductory arrangements. An enquiry helps you confirm those details; it does not reserve a place or commit you to a plan.
